dossier.summary: The paper asks what drives the error of regression-based GATE estimators under network interference. It splits the error into a design-leverage term and an extrapolation/misspecification bias, with closed forms for the one-hop fraction regression, and checks them in 6-world simulations on five synthetic graph families and two Facebook graphs. The main quantitative claims trace to delivered CSVs and scripts, and spot checks match. In particular, the closed-form leverage plus one fitted residual constant tracks the RMSE of the Bernoulli-design runs, and the bias formulas match simulation for Bernoulli p=1/2. Negative results (no closed form and a looser fit for cluster designs, biased boosting, anticonservative HAC, post-pilot estimators being in-sample) are stated openly. Weaker points: 'predictable from graph and design alone' needs a fitted constant that depends on the outcome scale; 'clustering helps in proportion to how well the graph clusters' is not tested and is contradicted within the Watts-Strogatz family; the Hájek baseline is only the full-neighbourhood variant. There are also small inconsistencies between text and files: the Monte-Carlo SE bound, the '20x' leverage, the 89% share, and Table 6 pooling ER runs across n. Uncertainty is shown as min-max over 6 worlds, not as confidence intervals, and the study does not cover the multi-stage designs, GNN regressors or dynamic graphs of the original study.

claims.quote: \textbf{Sampling error is predictable from graph and design alone.}
one fitted constant predicts the RMSE of 162 Bernoulli-design runs (median ratio $1.01$, $98\%$ within $10\%$)
the bias formulas match simulation to within about $0.01$--$0.02$ on a GATE of $2$
cluster randomization helps in proportion to how well the graph clusters

regression beats difference-in-means only when spillover exceeds $\approx\hat\kappa\sqrt{L/n}$

effect heterogeneity (OLS targets a $1/d_i$-weighted average of unit effects; Prop.~\ref{prop:wt}; bias up to $100\%$ of the GATE on Stanford3)
\textbf{Design matters as much as the estimator.}
H\'ajek estimators are undefined on dense random graphs ($d\ge32$) under unit randomization

issues.quote: cluster randomization helps in proportion to how well the graph clusters
issues.why: No test of proportionality is run, and within the Watts-Strogatz family the gain grows while clustering gets worse: cut fraction 6%->15% as the Bernoulli/cluster RMSE ratio rises 2.4->5.4 (verify_claims_output.txt, E1 ws_d). So the gain also depends on degree (d_H), and the claim holds only as a rough ranking across families.

issues.quote: \textbf{Sampling error is predictable from graph and design alone.}
issues.why: The prediction needs kappa-hat, fitted on simulated outcomes. Kappa scales with the outcome model: RMSE goes 0.065->0.503 as sigma_a goes 0.25->4 (Table 3). The 30 sigma_a-sweep runs were left out of the 162 runs (fig_variance.py/stats_summary.py filter tag!='er_siga'). The same sentence says 'one fitted constant'.

issues.quote: the bias formulas match simulation to within about $0.01$--$0.02$ on a GATE of $2$
issues.why: That accuracy holds for Bernoulli p=1/2. At p=0.05 the gap reaches 0.14-0.21 (Sec. 6.4), and cluster designs have no closed-form bias. Both are stated in the body, not next to the abstract claim.

issues.quote: H\'ajek estimators are undefined on dense random graphs ($d\ge32$) under unit randomization
issues.why: Only the full-neighbourhood exposure Hájek is implemented. Thresholded or fractional exposure definitions, which are standard for dense graphs, are not tried. Neither are the low-order or covariate-selection estimators the paper cites (the latter is conceded in Limitations). The 'undefined' result is a property of this one variant.

issues.quote: richer regressions help only where the graph supplies units with extreme exposures
issues.why: The evidence is an association across about six graph/design combinations: the extreme-exposure share against how well the cubic does. No experiment varies only the extreme-exposure share (for example, trimming those units) while keeping the graph and response fixed.

issues.quote: Monte-Carlo standard errors of each world's RMSE are $\le0.04\times$RMSE with $R=300$
issues.why: The result files disagree. In E1.csv, rmse_se/rmse for ols_s exceeds 0.04 in 48% of runs (max 0.19, cluster designs). In E5.csv it exceeds 0.06 in 9% of runs (max 0.49). For Bernoulli runs it is about 0.04-0.05, so the main claims are not affected.

issues.quote: their leverage was up to $20\times$ larger
issues.why: Sec. 6.3 itself reports leverage 3560 vs 121 (29x) for the two-step model. In E2.csv the cubic model's leverage is up to about 140x that of ols-s.

issues.quote: \emph{Pilot:} \textsc{wls-s}/\textsc{strat-s} were designed after the heterogeneity pilot, so Table~\ref{tab:het} is in-sample for them.
issues.why: The fixes were designed after seeing the pilot and are evaluated on the same worlds. Seeds are derived from the configuration, so pilot worlds 0-2 are part of the final 6. The paper states this, so it is minor.

issues.quote: with a nonlinear response fewer clusters are preferred (SBM $k{=}4$: $0.34$ at 40 clusters vs $0.46$ at 690)
issues.why: The RMSE is not monotone in the number of clusters. On SBM with k=4 it is 0.57 at 5 clusters and 0.47 at 10, both above the 0.34 at 40 (verify_claims_output.txt, K_pow4).

presentation.why: The reproducibility appendix lists script and function names (fig_variance.py, mk_tables.py:tab_het, experiments.stable_seed, code/graphs.py), and Appendix A names theory.py. Useful for reproduction, but these are traces of the working files inside the paper.
Appendix Tables 4-7 and Figures 6-7 float past the 'NeurIPS Paper Checklist' heading, onto pages 13-15 between checklist items.
Fig. 3(c) separates three estimators only by colour shade (dark/mid/light) and has no legend. Legends and tick labels in Figs. 1, 3 and 5 are about 5-6 pt and hard to read at print size.
There is no schematic of the setting (design -> exposures -> regression -> extrapolation to all-treated/all-control). The leverage/extrapolation idea is explained in text only.
Results paragraphs pack 20-30 numbers per paragraph (e.g. the flexible-regression paragraph), which makes the main point hard to follow.

paper_mismatches.why: The share is computed as a mean over all 378 rows, including 18 rows with an undefined RMSE that count as misses. Over the 360 world-settings the paper names, the share is about 93%.

tab_extrap does not filter E2 by tag. The ER/Bernoulli rows for k=4 and threshold average 24 world-runs over n=1000, 4000 (twice) and 16000 from the n_sweep, not 6 worlds at n=4000. RMSE 0.50 vs 0.49 (k=4), and bias +1.46 in the table vs +1.47 in the text (threshold).

paper_mismatches.paper_quote: Monte-Carlo standard errors of each world's RMSE are $\le0.04\times$RMSE with $R=300$
paper_mismatches.why: The code's own rmse_se column shows ratios above 0.04 in many runs (up to 0.19 in E1 and 0.49 in E5 cluster runs).

evaluation_errors.why: Table 6 ER/Bernoulli cells pool runs at different n (n_sweep tag), so the RMSE shown is not that of the n=4000 setting. Effect is at most about 0.01-0.02; no claim depends on it.

problems.why: Absolute paths /work/results, /work/paper/figs, /work/paper/tables and /work/data are hard-coded (experiments.py:13, ac.py:196-198, graphs.py:9,108, psi.py:182). Running from another location needs edits.
README and run_all_experiments.sh expect paper/ next to code/ (cd ../paper), but the delivery puts the paper under paper/source. Tables and figures are written to /work/paper.
The raw ego-Facebook archive and the Stanford3 zip are left out of the delivery (MANIFEST left_out). The script re-downloads them, and checksums are given.
run_all.sh says each experiment uses a 36-process pool; the code uses procs=4.

flagged.quantity: heterogeneity bias as share of GATE, Stanford3 inv
leverage of richer specifications relative to one-hop (max ratio, E3 two-step)
leverage deviation in median Bernoulli family

process_notes: The final experiments ran as detached nohup processes (steps 58, 74). fields.json says the record does not see their end; completion is inferred from log polling and file times.
Pilot runs (3 worlds, 36 processes) were killed and restarted after a crash fix and the 4-core quota was found (steps 24-56). The README and paper report this.
E3 was re-run after the post-pilot estimators wls-s/strat-s were added; the paper's E3 numbers and Table 1 were then refreshed (steps 149-154).
E7 was re-run at step 178 to check reproducibility; the output was bit-identical (step 179), as Appendix C states.
The whole span is about 1.9 h (19:16-21:12) in a single trajectory; the paper text was written while E5/E6/E3 were still running and then updated from verify_claims.py output.

integrity.why: No configuration is picked by its score as 'the method'. The paper proposes no estimator, and every specification's result is reported. kappa-hat is fitted on the 72 ER runs and checked on 90 non-ER runs, as the paper says. wls-s/strat-s were added after the pilot and tried on world 0 (step 73) before the full run. The paper states this and that Table 1 is in-sample for them.

Changes during the work: one-arm cluster draws are now redrawn (crash fix, stated in Sec. 3); seeds became hash-based; worlds went from 3 to 6; gbm moved to E2g; wls-s/strat-s were added (stated); and the sigma_a sweep was left out of the kappa fit/162-run check (step 49). That last one is noted under issues; it follows from kappa depending on the outcome scale, and Table 3 reports those runs.

The estimators use only z, the observed outcomes, graph features and design probabilities. The true tau and the unit parameters enter only the error metrics (sim.py:409-418) and the closed-form prediction columns (Prop. 4 B in mk_tables.tab_het), which are labelled as predictions.

The quoted numbers trace to E1-E7 outputs printed by verify_claims.py and stats_summary.py (steps 151, 187) or by analysis snippets (e.g. step 71 for the per-world Prop. 4 agreement). The real-graph crossover values (0.07, 0.12, 0.06, 0.19) were interpolated by hand from the printed E4 grid. No number lacks a run.
